analysis.one_liner: Requires federal licensing and fee disclosure for paid tax preparers and refund-advance products.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote and died at the end of the 113th Congress with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in charge of licensing paid tax return preparers who aren't already regulated as attorneys or CPAs, and of regulating refund anticipation arrangements — deals where a preparer or affiliated lender takes fees and interest out of a taxpayer's refund, often before the IRS even sends it. Preparers would have to show they are competent and honest, post their fee schedules, and warn customers that a refund advance isn't necessary to get a refund and that they still owe fees if the refund comes up short. The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income taxpayers who pay a commercial preparer to file their return or take out a refund advance — the customers most likely to be charged high fees for what is often a free, fast direct deposit from the IRS.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Filers who use paid tax preparers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require the CFPB to license or certify tax return preparers who are not already regulated under Title 31, and to make applicants demonstrate good character, qualifications, and competency before being allowed to prepare returns for pay [S2][S3].

It would require preparers to disclose their fee schedules, tell consumers how long an ordinary e-filed refund takes, explain how many extra days a refund advance costs them, state that a refund advance is not necessary to receive a refund, and warn that fees and interest are owed even if the refund is smaller than expected [S2][S3].

It would give the CFPB power to take enforcement action — after notice and a hearing — against preparers who are incompetent, disreputable, violate the rules, or knowingly mislead or threaten consumers [S2][S3].
It would close a Dodd-Frank loophole by striking the exclusion that had kept tax preparers outside the CFPB's coverage of preparer-related consumer products [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation chains and refund-advance lenders, who would face licensing fees, disclosure mandates, and potential enforcement actions, with some compliance costs likely passed to customers.

drawbacks.text: Licensing and certification fees would add compliance costs for small independent preparers, and some of that cost would likely be passed on to the low-income customers the bill is meant to protect [S2][S3].

The bill's refund-splitting provision would let a refund be deposited partly to the preparer at the taxpayer's request and would bar treating such a split as disreputable conduct merely because the taxpayer asked for it — a mechanism that could make it easier for preparers to collect their fees directly out of customers' refunds [S2][S3].

The disclosure rules rely on averages (average refund timing, average days saved), so individual customers could still face outcomes that look better or worse than the mandated statement suggests [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill targets a real, well-documented harm: refund-advance products that charge fees and interest — often at very high effective rates — to filers who could get the same money days later for free from the IRS. Mandatory competency standards and plain fee disclosures would help the customers least equipped to shop around. The tradeoffs are modest: some compliance cost for small preparers, and a refund-splitting mechanism that could entrench direct payment out of refunds. On balance, the consumer protections outweigh the burdens, though the split-refund provision sits awkwardly beside the bill's protective purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the Tax Refund Protection Act of 2014 on April 10, 2014, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].

The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means and to the Committee on Financial Services, in each case for consideration of the provisions within each committee's jurisdiction [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Paid tax preparation chains and refund-advance lenders are better off: they continued operating with no federal licensing standard, no required fee disclosures, and no CFPB enforcement, while the low-income filers who buy their products kept facing the same terms.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no documented opposition.

industries.industry: Commercial tax preparation chains and independent paid preparers
industries.note: The bill would have stripped their Dodd-Frank exemption, required CFPB licensing and competency testing, mandated fee disclosures, and allowed enforcement against preparers who mislead customers — cutting into fees earned from filers who often qualify for free IRS filing options.

industries.industry: Refund-advance lenders and banks affiliated with preparers
industries.note: Refund anticipation arrangements would have come under CFPB regulation and Truth in Lending-style rules, with disclosures showing how many extra days the product costs and warning that fees are owed even if the refund falls short — directly threatening the fee and interest income these products generate from taxpayers' own refunds.

industries.industry: Tax preparation industry (under the split-refund provision)
industries.note: Alongside the new rules, the bill would let a refund be split with the preparer at the taxpayer's request and would bar treating that split as disreputable conduct merely because the taxpayer asked — making it easier for preparers to be paid directly out of customers' refunds.
